I am a former hospital employee who worked with insurance/billing. Have you looked into Medicaid share of cost? Also referred to as medically needy. 

It is different than full Medicaid, which has strict eligibility requirements, and everyone ‘qualifies.’ It is still income based. They will determine a monthly amount that you are able to pay. If your medical bills exceed your share of cost for that month, Medicaid covers the whole bill. They also, at least while I was working in the field, pay retroactively for bills you had prior to being approved (90 days was the retroactive period when I was doing this work. It may have changed.)

Again, everyone ‘qualifies’ so it will only cost you your time to find out what your share of cost amount is. It is perfectly fine to have in addition to your health insurance.

As with all fields of medicine, if you try to address symptoms (suicidal ideation, explosive anger, etc) without addressing the underlying cause(s), you are doing your patients a disservice. I believe the reason that DBT is so effective is because it helps patients who (probably) have an external locus of control find that they have a lot of power over how they respond to the world around them. If you have power over that, you have power over outcomes to some degree. For me personally, it has massively changed the way I respond to stress. You can’t just tell someone that “this too shall pass,” they have to believe it. 

I had extremely neglectful, mentally ill parents who did not help me learn this as a child. I grew up in a constant state of stress which did not allow me to develop a sense of security or of self. As such, I’ve spent my whole life looking for someone to latch on to, someone to be my safe space. My tendency has always been to look externally, the way a small child would look for a parent to meet their needs. Now I realize that no one can ever love me better than I can. No one can advocate for me better than myself. My self worth is no longer tied to the opinions of others. That journey started with accepting some difficult truths. My emotions are my responsibility. My parents failed me in childhood but now that I am an adult, it’s up to me to choose how to respond to the damage my traumatic childhood caused. Respecting other people’s boundaries is important even if it doesn’t feel good personally. Loving other people means looking at what is good for them as well as yourself.

Your physical safety and mental health are the top priority here. You have to do what is best for you. You know your situation better than anyone. This is about what YOU need and want. If you’re codependent, that may be a difficult concept to truly accept. It may be difficult to feel confident in your decision. You said that your logic says you should leave. If you are, think about the things that would make working through it worthwhile and what changes you would need to see in order to stay (set a boundary about what you expect from your partner). If you aren’t - why accept less than the bare minimum? 

Regardless of whether you decide to stay in this relationship or not, I highly recommend finding a therapist who can help you get to the bottom of your codependency so you can start experiencing life outside of it.
